newsitem.title: UK: Dlr/mark steady above 1.75, awaits key jobs data.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/mark steady above 1.75, awaits key jobs data.

text.p: The dollar stuck to narrow ranges above 1.75 marks and 114 yen in early Europe, steady as the Federal Reserve held rates unchanged as expected and awaiting key U.S. data later on Thursday, said analysts.

A raft of economic data, including jobless and wage figures, could give the market fresh direction in the wake of the Fed's decision to leave rates steady on Wednesday amid signs economic growth has slowed from a sizzling first-quarter pace.
In the wake of the Fed's decision to leave rates unchanged - a move widely anticipated by markets - the focus is now firmly on the most-watched jobs and wage data at 1230 GMT.

At 0730 GMT dollar/mark stood at 1.7522/25 vs 1.7520/25 in late Europe on Wednesday and hovering just off fresh 40-month highs of 1.7550 marks hit on Wednesday. Dollar/yen was also steady at 114.31/4.36 against 114.38/4.43 in late Europe.

Non-farm payrolls are forecast to rise by 222,000 against 138,000 in May and average hourly earnings are forecast to rise by 0.4 percent. Other U.S. economic data on Thursday includes housing completions at 1400 GMT, jobless claims at 1230 GMT and money supply at 2030 GMT.
"It won't take much strong U.S. data to change market views," said Jesper Dannesboe, treasury economist at ABN AMRO.

Traders said with U.S. markets closed for the Independence Day celebrations on Friday, Thursday is expected to be a quiet day on currency markets -- with sterling attracting much of the attention in the wake of Wednesday's UK budget.
"It will be very quiet...Waiting for the minutes of the last Fed meeting and the unemployment figures, which could give the market a bit of a lift," said Peter Wood, forex dealer at Bank of Boston.
Overall, the dollar remains well bid in Europe as market fears of a soft euro and debate continues over how best to tackle budget overshoots in Germany and France, said economists.

Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber, for instance, reiterated on Wednesday his demand for a precise interpretation of the three percent government deficit to GDP entry criterion for Europe's planned single currency.
"If we now move away from three it will shake people's confidence," Stoiber told Germany's ARD television.
Stoiber said precisely hitting the 3.0 percent deficit to gross domestic product goal might not be decisive for economists, but it was for the majority of ordinary people.
Against the yen, the dollar was a touch pressured after comments by Bank of Japan (BOJ) Governor, said traders.

BOJ's Yasuo Matsushita said on Thursday the BOJ's monetary policy continued to be aimed at strengthening the basis for economic recovery. Asian traders, focused on a banker's convention, had been cautious during the meeting, but said his comments failed to surprise and therefore gave 10-year government bonds a helping hand.
However, senior Japanese traders on Thursday said Japan may be ready to raise rates in the fourth-quarter if private demand keeps fuelling economic recovery in the next three months.

Elsewhere, sterling remained the darling of currency markets as it banked on higher UK rates in the wake of the UK budget. At 0900 GMT, it was orbiting around 2.94 marks and eyeing its old European exchange-rate mechanism (EM) parity rate of 2.95 marks.
